title: Sisyphus: eternal punishment
subtitle: The rock that always rolls back
subject: mythologie
description: Sisyphus cheats Death, then the gods themselves. His sentence: roll a rock that always falls back. Camus turned him into the symbol of clear sight in the face of the absurd.

hero.hook: He cheated Death. The gods gave him a rock. And eternity to push it.

blocks.text: **Sisyphus**, the legendary founder of Corinth, is the craftiest mortal in Greek myth. His intelligence let him defy the gods. It also earned him the worst punishment of all: an effort that never gets anywhere.

In the 20th century, **Albert Camus** turned this condemned man into a figure of the human condition. From ancient cunning to modern revolt, Sisyphus asks one simple question: what do you do when the goal looks impossible?

[[Homer]] calls him the craftiest of men. Sisyphus saw **Zeus**, king of the gods, carry off the nymph **Aegina**. Instead of keeping quiet, he sold the secret to the girl's father, the river god [[Asopus]], in exchange for a spring of fresh water for his citadel.

blocks.caption: Sisyphus, the cunning king of Corinth

blocks.text: Zeus sent **Thanatos**, Death in person. Sisyphus pretended to admire his chains, asked for a demonstration, and then locked Death up in them. While Thanatos lay tied, nobody on Earth could die. Even the soldiers of **Ares**, god of war, stayed on their feet. Ares had to free Thanatos by force.
Some linguists connect the name “Sisyphus” with the Greek *sophos*, “wise.” If they are right, his name means “the very wise one”, a cruel joke against his fate.

Before dying, Sisyphus ordered his wife **Merope** to give him no funeral rites. Down in the Underworld, he complained to **Persephone**, queen of the dead: his wife had dishonored him. He won three days on Earth to put it right. Once back in the sunlight, he refused to return.

**Hermes**, messenger of the gods and guide of souls, dragged him back to [[Hades]]. The punishment was made to measure: push a huge rock to the top of a hill. Every time, just short of the summit, the stone rolled back down.
In some ancient traditions, the rock of Sisyphus explained the cycle of the tides or the daily movement of the sun.

Unlike [[Prometheus]], whose liver is eaten day after day, Sisyphus takes no wound in the flesh. His torture is uselessness. In **1942**, Camus published *The Myth of Sisyphus*. For him, Sisyphus is the [[absurd hero]]: he knows the rock will roll back down, and that clear sight is exactly what makes him great.
Psychiatry has sometimes used the word “Sisyphism” for the repetition of exhausting, pointless actions.

The [[absurd in Camus and Sisyphus]] is the clash between our need for meaning and the silence of the world. Each time he walks back down the mountain, Sisyphus takes up the task again. His revolt is to keep going with his eyes open. “One must imagine Sisyphus happy.”

The phrase “a labor of Sisyphus” means a hard, repetitive, pointless task. In the modern world the myth speaks to assembly line workers and to office staff caught in endless procedures. [[The hubris of Sisyphus]], the wish to outwit the gods, is also a lesson about where cunning stops.

Yet the story keeps its power: the failure is announced in advance, and the effort goes on anyway. The rock rolls back, but it does not erase the climb. Sisyphus lasts because he stands for resilience in the face of a fate that promises no victory.
**Sisyphus** cheated Death and the gods, then pushed a rock for eternity. **Camus** turned him into the symbol of clear sight: know the absurd, and keep going anyway.
